text: Soil pH measures acidity or alkalinity. Most crops grow well between pH 6 and 7.5. Values below 5.5 indicate strong acidity; above 8.5 indicate alkalinity. Adjust with lime (raise pH) or sulfur (lower pH).
Nitrogen supports leaf growth and chlorophyll production. Deficiency causes yellowing of older leaves. Recommended for leafy crops in split doses. Sources: urea, ammonium sulfate, organic manure.
Phosphorus supports root development, energy transfer, and flowering. Low availability in alkaline soils. Apply near root zone for better uptake. Sources: DAP, SSP, rock phosphate.
Potassium regulates water movement, enzyme activation, and stress tolerance. Deficient plants show scorched leaf edges. Important for fruiting crops. Sources: MOP (muriate of potash), SOP.
Compost, farmyard manure, and green manures improve soil structure, water retention, and nutrient cycling. Aim for 2-4% organic carbon content for healthy soil.
Soil moisture affects nutrient availability and root respiration. Optimal range varies by crop; most need 50-70% of field capacity. Monitor with tensiometers or soil moisture sensors.
Loamy soil is a balanced mix of sand, silt, and clay. Offers good drainage and water retention. Best for most crops including vegetables and cereals.
Clay soils retain water and nutrients but drain slowly and compact easily. Improve with organic matter, gypsum, and raised beds.
Sandy soils drain quickly and hold fewer nutrients. Require frequent irrigation and organic matter addition for better fertility.
Soil tests measure pH, electrical conductivity, organic carbon, and available N-P-K. Sample from 15 cm depth for accurate results. Test every 2-3 years.
Apply fertilizers based on soil test results, crop requirement, and growth stage. Avoid over-application which can cause nutrient burn or runoff.
Zinc, iron, boron, manganese, and copper are needed in small amounts. Deficiency symptoms appear on specific plant parts. Soil testing prevents toxicity.
Soil salinity restricts water uptake. Test electrical conductivity (EC). Manage with drainage, gypsum, and salt-tolerant crops like barley and cotton.
Waterlogging reduces oxygen to roots, causing yellowing and root rot. Improve with drainage, raised beds, and avoiding over-irrigation.
Rice grows in warm, humid conditions with abundant water. Best soil pH is 5.5-6.5. Requires high nitrogen and potassium. Grown in kharif season.
Wheat is a cool-season crop. Ideal pH 6.0-7.5. Requires moderate nitrogen, good phosphorus for root development, and adequate potassium. Grown in rabi season.
Maize needs warm temperatures, well-drained loamy soil, and pH 5.8-7.0. Heavy nitrogen feeder, especially during vegetative stage.
Pulses like chickpea and lentil fix nitrogen and improve soil health. Require less nitrogen but need phosphorus and potassium for pod formation.
Tomatoes need well-drained soil, pH 6.0-6.8, and consistent moisture. High potassium and calcium prevent blossom-end rot.
Potatoes prefer loose, well-drained soil with pH 5.0-6.0. Requires high potassium for tuber development and moderate nitrogen.
Cotton grows best in black soil with pH 6.0-8.0. Requires moderate nitrogen, high potassium, and warm temperatures with adequate rainfall.
Sugarcane needs deep, well-drained loamy soil with pH 6.5-7.5. Heavy feeder requiring high nitrogen and potassium through the growth cycle.
Signs: pale green to yellow older leaves, stunted growth. Fix: apply urea or ammonium sulfate. Use 50 kg N/ha for most cereals.
Signs: dark green or purple leaves, poor root development, delayed flowering. Fix: apply DAP or SSP near root zone.
Signs: scorched or brown leaf edges, weak stems, poor fruit quality. Fix: apply MOP at 40-60 kg K2O/ha.
